chapter.name: Arithmetic Expressions
chapter.blurb: Writing and comparing expressions, terms, commutative/associative properties, brackets, and the distributive property.

scope: IN
Write an arithmetic expression modelling a real situation (money, marbles, tickets, repeated events)
IN
Recognise that different expressions can share the same value
IN
Compare two expressions with =, < or > by reasoning about structure, not full computation
IN
Identify the terms of an expression, converting each subtraction to 'add the inverse' first
IN
Apply the commutative property of addition to terms (swap order without changing the value)
IN
Apply the associative property of addition to terms (regroup without changing the value)
IN
Evaluate an expression by computing each x/division term first, then adding all terms in any order
IN
Evaluate an expression with a single level of brackets, innermost-first
IN
Remove a bracket preceded by '+' without changing the signs of the terms inside
IN
Remove a bracket preceded by '-', correctly flipping the sign of every term inside
IN
Apply the distributive property to expand a x (b+-c) into a x b +- a x c
IN
Apply the distributive property in reverse to factor a common multiplier out of a sum/difference
IN
Use the distributive property as a mental-math shortcut (e.g. 97x25 via (100-3)x25)
OUT

BODMAS/PEMDAS as a named acronym or memorised rule order -- The chapter deliberately teaches order-of-operations via "terms", never names or drills an acronym -- a generated question must not lean on BODMAS terminology
OUT
Algebraic expressions with a variable (x, y, n as an unknown) -- This chapter is purely numeric; variables are introduced in a later chapter
OUT
Solving an equation for an unknown value -- This chapter only evaluates and compares given expressions -- no "solve for x"
OUT
Exponents or powers inside an expression -- Not introduced in this chapter
OUT
Fractions or decimals as the numbers inside an expression -- All worked examples use whole numbers/integers; decimals belong to Chapter 3 (A Peek Beyond the Point)
OUT
Nested brackets more than one level deep, e.g. ((a+b)-(c-d)) -- Every worked example and Figure-it-Out item uses at most one level of brackets
OUT

New rules for multiplying/dividing negative numbers -- The chapter explicitly assumes the Token Model of integers from Class 6 as prior knowledge; it only builds addition/subtraction of terms on top of it
OUT
Algebraic identities beyond the distributive property, e.g. (a+b) squared -- Not covered anywhere in this chapter

concepts.name: Writing and comparing simple expressions
concepts.description: Modelling a real situation as an expression, and comparing two expressions with =, < or > by reasoning rather than full computation.
concepts.idea: An arithmetic expression is a phrase like 5 x 25 that has a value; different expressions can share the same value, and two expressions can be compared by reasoning about the situation rather than always calculating in full.
concepts.rule: Model a real situation as an expression first; to compare two expressions, look at how their parts differ rather than computing both from scratch.
concepts.example: Mallika spends Rs.25/day for lunch, Mon-Fri: 5 x 25. Comparing 1023+125 and 1022+128 by reasoning: Raja started 1 marble ahead but gained 3 fewer, so Joy ends 2 ahead -- 1023+125 < 1022+128.

concepts.name: Terms of an expression
concepts.description: Identifying the terms of an expression by rewriting every subtraction as 'add the inverse' first.
concepts.idea: The terms of an expression are its parts separated by a '+' sign; every subtraction is first rewritten as 'add the inverse' so the whole expression becomes a sum of terms.
concepts.rule: Rewrite a - b as a + (-b) before identifying terms. A part containing x or / with no + inside it is a single term.
concepts.example: 83 - 14 = 83 + -14, so the terms are 83 and -14. In 6 x 5 + 3, the terms are (6x5) and 3.

concepts.name: Commutative and associative property of addition (of terms)
concepts.description: Swapping or regrouping the terms of an expression never changes its value, even with negative terms.
concepts.idea: Once an expression is written as a sum of terms, the terms can be swapped (commutative) or regrouped (associative) in any order without changing the value -- this holds even when some terms are negative.
concepts.rule: Term1 + Term2 = Term2 + Term1. (Term1+Term2)+Term3 = Term1+(Term2+Term3). Applies to any number of terms, in any order.
concepts.example: (-7) + 10 + (-11) gives -8 however the three terms are grouped or reordered.

concepts.name: Evaluating expressions with brackets and mixed operations
concepts.description: Evaluating brackets first, then each multiplication/division term, then adding all terms.
concepts.idea: A bracketed sub-expression is evaluated first. Without brackets, an expression is evaluated by first finding the value of each term (a term with x or / is computed as one unit), then adding all the terms.
concepts.rule: Evaluate innermost brackets first; then evaluate each remaining multiplication/division term; then add all terms in any order.

concepts.name: Removing brackets (sign changes)
concepts.description: The sign-flip rule for removing a bracket preceded by a minus sign, versus a plus sign.
concepts.idea: A bracket preceded by '-' flips the sign of every term inside it when removed; a bracket preceded by '+' (or nothing) leaves the signs unchanged.
concepts.rule: a - (b + c) = a - b - c. a - (b - c) = a - b + c. a + (b - c) = a + b - c (signs unchanged).

concepts.name: Distributive property
concepts.description: Multiplying a number by a sum/difference equals the sum/difference of the products, and the reverse (factoring).
concepts.idea: Multiplying a number by a sum or difference gives the same result as multiplying it by each term separately and then adding/subtracting -- and the reverse: a common multiplier can be factored back out.
concepts.rule: a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c. a x (b - c) = a x b - a x c. Works in both directions (expanding and factoring).
concepts.example: 4 x 5 + 3 x 5 = (4+3) x 5 = 35 (scouts and guides). 2 x (43+24) = 2x43 + 2x24 (bill split).

concepts.name: Real-world modelling and mental-math shortcuts
concepts.description: Modelling word problems as expressions, and using the distributive property as a quick-multiplication trick.
concepts.idea: Real situations (money, tickets, repeated events) are modelled as expressions using terms, brackets and the distributive property; the same property gives quick ways to multiply numbers close to a round number.
concepts.rule: To multiply near a round number, rewrite one factor as (round number +/- small number) and distribute.
concepts.example: 97 x 25 = (100-3) x 25 = 2500-75 = 2425. Binu's yearly savings from a monthly budget: (20000-5000-5000-2000) x 12.
